```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

Does chilling reduce carbon dioxide uptake, and does the answer depend on
carbon dioxide concentration or plant origin? When does increasing concentration
produce the largest increase in uptake? These questions require comparisons of
fitted responses and their rates of change, rather than inspection of individual
smooths alone. This article uses the same model to answer each question and to
explain how the choice of interval changes the conclusion.

The examples use the `CO2` dataset distributed with R, plus {mgcv}, {gratia},
{dplyr} and {ggplot2}. We use 2,000 coefficient draws for the bands and
posterior calculations.
If a conclusion depends on an interval limit, increase this count and check
that the limit is stable. We load the packages before preparing the data.

```{r packages, message=FALSE}
library("gratia")
load_mgcv()
library("dplyr")
library("ggplot2")
```

## Fit treatment curves to the plant experiment

The `CO2` data come from an experiment on cold tolerance in *Echinochloa
crus-galli*. The researchers measured uptake at seven concentrations in each of
twelve plants, with three plants per combination of origin and treatment. The
chilled plants were cooled during the day and allowed to recover overnight
before measurement. Uptake is measured in micromoles per square metre per
second. The original study reports `conc` in microlitres per litre
($\mu\mathrm{L}\,\mathrm{L}^{-1}$), which we use for the axes and rates of
change below. [Potvin et al. (1990)](https://doi.org/10.2307/1938276)

```{r data-and-observations}
plant <- as.data.frame(datasets::CO2)
plant$Plant <- factor(plant$Plant, ordered = FALSE)

uptake_label <- expression(CO[2]~uptake~(mu*mol~m^{-2}~s^{-1}))
concentration_label <- expression(
  Ambient ~ CO[2] ~ concentration ~ (mu * L ~ L^{-1})
)

ggplot(plant, aes(conc, uptake, colour = Treatment, group = Plant)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ Type) +
  labs(x = concentration_label, y = uptake_label, colour = "Treatment")
```

Uptake increases quickly at lower concentrations and then tends to level off.
The chilled Mississippi plants have particularly low uptake. We fit a separate
smooth concentration response for each treatment, and allow the treatment
contrast in average log uptake to differ by origin. A plant random intercept
allows measurements from the same plant to share a persistent deviation from
the fitted curve.

All responses are positive. The log link ensures positive fitted means, and
the Gamma model assumes that residual standard deviation is proportional to
the mean. On the log scale the model uses the same concentration smooth for
both origins within a treatment. The origin-by-treatment interaction allows
the difference in curve height between origins to vary by treatment. Sharing
smooths lets both origins inform the estimated shape for each treatment.

```{r fit-model}
m_uptake <- gam(
  uptake ~ Type * Treatment + s(conc, by = Treatment, k = 5) +
    s(Plant, bs = "re"),
  data = plant, family = Gamma(link = "log"), method = "REML"
)
overview(m_uptake)
```

`k = 5` sets the basis dimension for each treatment smooth. REML estimates
how strongly to penalise wiggliness within that basis. The plant intercept
accounts for persistent differences in curve height. Residual patterns against
concentration can show whether plant differences also involve curve shape.
See the [diagnostic workflow](model-checking.html) for checks with fitted and
simulated effects. The experiment paired chilled and control plants within
each origin. This example accounts for the seven repeated measurements per
plant and treats plants as independent in the model. An analysis using the
full experimental design would also account for the pairing.

## Compare expected uptake over the observed concentration range

For each origin and treatment, evaluate concentration across its observed
range. `.by` evaluates expressions within observed groups. This matters when
groups have different ranges: using the overall range can extrapolate for
some groups. Here the experimental concentration range is the same in all
four groups.

```{r grouped-grid}
uptake_grid <- data_slice(m_uptake,
  conc = evenly(conc, n = 60),
  Plant = level(Plant, as.character(Plant[1])),
  .by = c(Type, Treatment)
)
uptake_grid |>
  group_by(Type, Treatment) |>
  summarise(lower = min(conc), upper = max(conc), .groups = "drop")
```

The `Plant` expression supplies one actual plant identifier in each group.
We set its random effect to zero with `exclude = "s(Plant)"`, so every curve
describes expected uptake for a plant with a zero random intercept. Averaging
over the population of plants would give a higher expected uptake because a
positive random intercept raises uptake by more than an equally large negative
intercept lowers it. The bands describe uncertainty in the curves of expected
uptake. Prediction intervals for new measurements would also include variation
around those curves.

```{r predictions-and-bands}
uptake_fitted <- fitted_values(m_uptake,
  data = uptake_grid, exclude = "s(Plant)",
  interval = "simultaneous", n_sim = 2000, seed = 2026
)

ggplot(uptake_fitted, aes(conc, .fitted, colour = Treatment, fill = Treatment)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = .lower_ci, ymax = .upper_ci), alpha = 0.2,
    colour = NA) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~ Type) +
  labs(x = concentration_label, y = uptake_label,
    colour = "Treatment", fill = "Treatment")
```

The fitted Mississippi curves are lower, especially after chilling. For the
Quebec plants the treatment curves are closer. Overlap between two prediction
bands is not a direct test of their difference: both curves depend on the same
estimated coefficients, and their errors are correlated.

The default `interval = "confidence"` gives a separate pointwise interval at
each row. `interval = "simultaneous"` constructs one band with approximate
posterior coverage across all 240 supplied rows together, including both
origins and treatments. This joint coverage applies to the evaluated rows.
`fitted_values()` constructs the band on the link scale and then transforms
the limits to the uptake scale. The returned `.se` is on the link scale.

## Estimate the treatment difference directly

`conditional_differences()` compares whole-model predictions, including the
parametric origin and treatment effects. Put `Treatment` in `by` and `Type` in
`condition` to compare treatments *within* each origin.

```{r treatment-differences}
treatment_difference <- conditional_differences(m_uptake,
  by = "Treatment", condition = c("conc", "Type"),
  exclude = "s(Plant)", scale = "response",
  uncertainty = "delta", interval = "simultaneous",
  simultaneous_scope = "contrast", n_vals = 60, n_sim = 2000, seed = 2026
)
draw(treatment_difference) +
  labs(x = concentration_label,
    y = "Expected uptake: nonchilled minus chilled")
```

The factor level order makes this the nonchilled mean minus the chilled mean.
A positive difference means lower expected uptake after chilling. Where the
band lies above zero, the fitted model supports a positive difference. It does
so over much of the concentration range in Mississippi, with weaker evidence
in Quebec. The band covers concentrations for both origins jointly because
there is one treatment contrast.

The default delta method uses a linear approximation to how changes in the
coefficients affect predicted differences on the response scale. We next apply
the inverse link to the predictions from each draw and then take the difference.
This can give asymmetric intervals on the response scale.

```{r posterior-differences}
treatment_simulation <- conditional_differences(m_uptake,
  by = "Treatment",
  condition = list(conc = c(250, 500, 750), "Type"),
  exclude = "s(Plant)", scale = "response", uncertainty = "simulation",
  n_sim = 2000, seed = 2026
)
treatment_simulation
```

For each posterior draw, gratia predicts both treatments with the **same**
coefficient vector and subtracts within that draw. Sampling treatments
independently would lose their covariance. These pointwise intervals are
equal-tailed posterior quantiles; they need not be symmetric about `.diff`,
which is always the difference of the fitted predictions.

The choice of what is covered jointly matters when comparing more than two
groups. Putting both factors in `by` compares all four combinations of origin
and treatment, giving six pairwise contrasts. `simultaneous_scope = "contrast"`
constructs a separate band for each pair across the concentration grid. Choose
`"all"` if you plan to inspect all six comparisons and want joint coverage
across both the pairs and the concentrations.

```{r all-group-comparisons}
all_differences <- conditional_differences(m_uptake,
  by = c("Type", "Treatment"), condition = "conc", exclude = "s(Plant)",
  uncertainty = "simulation", interval = "simultaneous",
  simultaneous_scope = "all", n_vals = 60, n_sim = 2000, seed = 2026
)
all_differences |>
  group_by(.contrast, Type_1, Treatment_1, Type_2, Treatment_2) |>
  slice_min(abs(conc - 500), n = 1) |>
  ungroup()
```

Simultaneous simulation bands are symmetric about `.diff`; their widths are
chosen for joint coverage. Both uncertainty methods describe differences in
mean responses, excluding observation noise. `conditional_differences()`
supports ordinary GAM and BAM families with one linear predictor, including
Gamma, negative binomial and Tweedie. Families with several linear predictors
remain unsupported.

The same comparisons are available for supported {scam} models. Their intervals
condition on the fitted smoothing parameters, so retain `unconditional = FALSE`.
The [scam article](scam-support.html) explains the coefficient transformations
used for their analytic intervals and simulation draws.

### Compare shape separately from complete responses

To ask whether the *centred smooth shapes* differ, use `difference_smooths()`.
This omits parametric treatment and origin effects by default.

```{r smooth-shape-comparison}
shape_difference <- difference_smooths(m_uptake, select = "s(conc)",
  interval = "simultaneous", n = 60, n_sim = 2000, seed = 2026
)
draw(shape_difference) +
  labs(x = concentration_label, y = "Difference of centred log-uptake smooths")
```

Much of this band contains zero. Thus the marked difference in expected
Mississippi uptake need not imply a comparably marked difference in smooth
shape. `group_means = TRUE` can add the means for the smooth's grouping factor,
but for this model the origin-by-treatment interaction makes whole-model
`conditional_differences()` the clearer choice. Smooth differences remain on
the link scale, with simultaneous coverage separately for each pair; they do
not provide joint coverage across several pairs.

## Where does uptake change fastest?

The derivative of expected uptake measures how much the mean response changes
for a small increase in concentration, in uptake units per concentration unit.
We compare delta-method and simulation intervals while holding origin and
treatment fixed. Evaluation points lie inside the observed range so the
finite differences do not require predictions beyond its endpoints.

```{r response-rates}
rate_grid <- data_slice(m_uptake,
  conc = evenly(conc, n = 60, lower = 110, upper = 990),
  Type = level(Type, "Quebec"),
  Treatment = level(Treatment, "nonchilled")
)
rate_delta <- response_derivatives(m_uptake,
  focal = "conc", data = rate_grid, type = "central",
  uncertainty = "delta", exclude = "s(Plant)"
)
rate_simulation <- response_derivatives(m_uptake,
  focal = "conc", data = rate_grid, type = "central",
  uncertainty = "simulation", n_sim = 2000, seed = 2026,
  exclude = "s(Plant)"
)
rates <- bind_rows(delta = rate_delta, simulation = rate_simulation,
  .id = "Uncertainty")
ggplot(rates, aes(conc, .derivative, colour = Uncertainty, fill = Uncertainty)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = .lower_ci, ymax = .upper_ci), alpha = 0.15,
    colour = NA) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = concentration_label,
    y = expression("Change in expected uptake per" ~ mu * L ~ L^{-1}))
```

For the nonchilled Quebec curve, the fastest fitted increase is at low
concentrations; further increases have a smaller effect over much of the
remaining range. The spline also has local decreases: this fit has no
monotonicity or asymptote constraint. Near the upper end, intervals include
zero, so the estimated small changes have no clearly supported direction.

Both methods return **pointwise** derivative intervals and `.se`. Delta
uncertainty uses the finite difference of fitted predictions and normal
intervals; simulation uses the median and quantiles of derivative draws.
The plotted methods agree closely where uncertainty is modest. Differences
can grow when the inverse link strongly transforms uncertain coefficients.
Delta uncertainty supports single-predictor GAM/BAM families and SCAM fits.
For SCAM fits it uses the transformed-coefficient covariance, conditional on
the fitted smoothing parameters. General families with several predictors
do not support delta uncertainty; their existing simulation support is unchanged.

The default `eps = NULL` chooses the perturbation from the fitted covariate
range, derivative order and finite-difference method. This reduces dependence
on measurement units and avoids many rounding problems in second derivatives.
It is a heuristic: near a domain boundary or with unusual scales, supply a
positive absolute `eps` and check stability using nearby values. Set `order = 2`
to estimate curvature; the first derivative above is the rate of uptake change.

## Plot transformed covariates and differentiate in the intended units

An alternative model uses a smooth of log concentration. The log transformation
stretches differences among lower concentrations, where uptake changes quickly.
This example also uses a common concentration smooth across treatments. We use
it to show how a transformed covariate affects the plotting coordinates and
derivative units.

```{r transformed-model}
m_log_conc <- gam(
  uptake ~ Type * Treatment + s(log(conc), k = 6) + s(Plant, bs = "re"),
  data = plant, family = Gamma(link = "log"), method = "REML"
)
draw(m_log_conc, select = "s(log(conc))", back_transform = TRUE,
  envir = environment()) +
  labs(x = concentration_label, y = "Centred contribution to log uptake")
```

`back_transform = TRUE` displays concentration in its original units. It
changes the horizontal axis, not the meaning of the partial effect on the
vertical axis. `smooth_estimates(..., back_transform = TRUE)` also generates
a grid evenly spaced in the raw covariate. The default grid is evenly spaced
in `log(conc)`. Supply raw `conc` values in `data` for predictions; gratia
evaluates the expression.

Here `envir = environment()` identifies the article's evaluation environment
so the original `plant` data can be recovered even when the model's stored
formula environment does not locate them. This is useful in notebooks and
within fitting functions as well as for custom transformations.

The same coordinate choice applies to parametric effects. For comparison,
a model containing a linear `log(conc)` term assumes a constant log-uptake
change per proportional concentration change. It cannot represent the
plateau as flexibly as a smooth:

```{r parametric-coordinates}
m_log_linear <- gam(
  uptake ~ Type * Treatment + log(conc) + s(Plant, bs = "re"),
  data = plant, family = Gamma(link = "log"), method = "REML"
)
linear_effect <- parametric_effects(m_log_linear, terms = "log(conc)",
  data = rate_grid, envir = environment())
draw(linear_effect, back_transform = TRUE) +
  labs(x = concentration_label, y = "Contribution to log uptake")
```

The horizontal axis uses concentration, while the effect remains a
contribution to log uptake. Drawing the same object with
`back_transform = FALSE` uses log concentration without changing the estimates.
The straight relationship in log concentration appears curved when drawn
against concentration in its original units.

For a smooth of log concentration, the derivative can be taken with respect
to either log concentration or concentration itself. We compute both and use
the chain rule to check that they agree after converting units.

```{r transformed-rates}
log_coordinate_rate <- derivatives(m_log_conc,
  select = "s(log(conc))", data = rate_grid, type = "central"
)
concentration_rate <- derivatives(m_log_conc,
  select = "s(log(conc))", data = rate_grid, type = "central",
  wrt = "covariate"
)
data.frame(conc = rate_grid$conc,
  derivative_per_concentration = concentration_rate$.derivative,
  derivative_per_log_concentration_divided_by_conc =
    log_coordinate_rate$.derivative / rate_grid$conc) |>
  slice(c(1, 20, 40, 60))
```

For a smooth contribution $f(\log c)$ the chain rule gives
$df/dc = (df/d\log c)/c$. The two columns agree up to numerical approximation.
Both concern the smooth's contribution to **log uptake**, not uptake itself.
`response_derivatives(..., focal = "conc")` differentiates complete fitted
responses in raw concentration units instead. For tensor smooths such as
`te(log(conc), temperature)`, use `partial_derivatives()` with
`wrt = "covariate", focal = "conc"` while holding temperature fixed.
See [Predictions, plots and derivatives with transformed covariates](transformed-covariates.html)
for worked tensor, transformed-offset and local-function examples. Preserve
the fitting environment, or pass `envir`, if expressions need local functions
or constants at new data.

## Keep each plant with its observed origin and treatment

`all_levels()` is a clearly named alias of `evenly()` for factors. It keeps
their fitted levels, which is useful when deliberately requesting a full
factor grid. Such a grid is not always scientifically sensible: each plant
in this experiment belongs to only one origin and treatment.

```{r observed-factor-combinations}
all_levels(plant$Treatment)
observed_plants <- conditional_values(m_uptake,
  condition = c("conc", "Plant", "Treatment", "Type"),
  n_vals = 7, complete = FALSE
)
observed_plants |>
  distinct(Plant, Treatment, Type)
```

`complete = FALSE` keeps only the observed combinations of the *conditioned*
factors, here the twelve actual plants with their assigned origin and
treatment. It still creates a numeric concentration grid; it does not restrict
predictions to measured concentrations, or to a joint region of support for
continuous covariates. Include every factor whose combinations need restricting.
An omitted factor is still held at its typical value.

`fitted_values()` reports rows containing combinations of known categorical
levels absent from the fitting data. Treat that message as a prompt to examine
the prediction design. For example, plant Qn1 was never a chilled Mississippi
plant:

```{r categorical-prediction-message}
hypothetical_grid <- data_slice(m_uptake,
  conc = 500, Type = level(Type, "Mississippi"),
  Treatment = level(Treatment, "chilled"), Plant = level(Plant, "Qn1")
)
fitted_values(m_uptake, data = hypothetical_grid, exclude = "s(Plant)")
```

The message checks categorical combinations even when a responsible term is
excluded. In the earlier treatment contrast, holding a plant
identifier fixed while excluding `s(Plant)` is intentional: its contribution
is zero in both scenarios. When predicting for an observed plant with its
random effect included, use that plant's assigned origin and treatment.

### Preserve observation positions when measurements are missing

With `na.exclude()`, results evaluated on the fitting data restore excluded rows
as `NA`. This keeps predictions aligned with the original observation records.
For illustration, remove one measured response and refit:

```{r missing-observation}
plant_missing <- plant
plant_missing$uptake[1] <- NA_real_
m_missing <- gam(
  uptake ~ Type * Treatment + s(conc, by = Treatment, k = 5) +
    s(Plant, bs = "re"),
  data = plant_missing, family = Gamma(link = "log"), method = "REML",
  na.action = na.exclude
)
fitted_missing <- fitted_values(m_missing)
fitted_missing |>
  mutate(uptake = plant_missing$uptake) |>
  slice_head(n = 3)
```

The first observation was excluded from fitting, so its default fitted result
is missing. In contrast, explicit prediction data with a missing response
can still give a fitted mean when their predictors are present:

```{r missing-prediction-values}
prediction_missing <- plant_missing[1:3, ]
prediction_missing$conc[2] <- NA_real_
fitted_values(m_missing, data = prediction_missing)
```

The first prediction is available; the second has a missing required predictor
and retains its row with an `NA` result. `na.omit()` retains only fitting rows
instead. Partial residuals, fitted/posterior samples and simulations likewise
respect `na.exclude()` positions; diagnostic functions align the retained
observations before checking their distributions.

## Choose the coefficient covariance for intervals

The examples use mgcv's approximate Bayesian coefficient covariance, conditional
on estimated smoothing parameters. `unconditional = TRUE` requests the
correction for smoothing-parameter uncertainty when it is available.
`get_vcov()` exposes the same matrix for custom calculations:

```{r covariance-choice}
V <- get_vcov(m_uptake)
dim(V)
dim(get_vcov(m_uptake, term = "s(conc):Treatmentnonchilled"))
```

For functions that provide `frequentist`, including `difference_smooths()`,
`derivatives()` and `smooth_estimates()`, setting it to `TRUE` selects the
covariance of the penalised coefficient estimators instead. This describes
their sampling variability, while the default covariance supplies the
approximate posterior intervals used above.
`get_vcov(..., frequentist = TRUE)` gives that matrix,
and `get_vcov(..., term = "s(conc):Treatmentnonchilled")` extracts a term's
coefficient covariance. Keeping the full matrix is essential when comparing
two terms whose estimates are correlated.

Distribution parameters and link functions also require explicit choices in
models with several predictors. For example, `link(gaulss(), parameter = "location")`
selects the mean's link, whereas `inv_link(gaulss(), parameter = "scale")`
selects the scale predictor's inverse link:

```{r parameter-links}
link(gaulss(), parameter = "location")(c(1, 2))
inv_link(gaulss(), parameter = "scale")(c(-1, 0, 1))
```

The functions follow the fitting package's parameterisation. As explained in
the [mgcv gaulss documentation](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/mgcv/html/gaulss.html),
the second inverse link returns **inverse standard deviation**, so it should
not be labelled standard deviation without taking its reciprocal. These
utilities do not remove the multiple-predictor restrictions of the comparison
or delta derivative methods.
